qs.q: Which inheritance pattern typically shows that the trait does not affect parents but may affect siblings?
o: Dominant inheritance linked to the X chromosome
Recessive inheritance on autosomes requiring two copies
qs.e: Autosomal recessive inheritance typically shows unaffected parents (both carriers) with affected siblings, as the trait requires two copies of the mutant allele to manifest.

qs.q: : Vitamin D-resistant rickets represents which unusual inheritance pattern?
o: Inherited via an X-linked dominant pattern
Followed by an autosomal recessive pattern
qs.e: Vitamin D-resistant rickets is one of the few X-linked dominant conditions, making it an exception to the rule that almost all X-linked disorders are recessive.

qs.q: : Almost all inborn errors of metabolism follow which inheritance pattern?
qs.e: Almost all inborn errors of metabolism are autosomal recessive disorders, where enzyme deficiencies manifest only in the homozygous recessive state.

qs.q: A child born to phenotypically normal parents develops cystic fibrosis. The inheritance pattern is most consistent with: Two unaffected carrier parents having an affected child is the hallmark of autosomal recessive inheritance. ---
qs.e: An affected child born to two unaffected carrier parents is the characteristic hallmark of autosomal recessive inheritance.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Inheritance patterns describe how genetic variants are transmitted across generations and shape disease risk. Recognizing dominant, recessive, X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance guides history taking, testing and counseling.

sections.p: Genes are passed from parents to offspring in predictable ways. Patterns determine who may be affected, carrier status, and recurrence risk for families.
b: Autosomal dominant: one mutant allele causes disease; vertical transmission.
Autosomal recessive: two mutant alleles required; often seen in siblings.
X-linked dominant/recessive: sex chromosome location influences risk.

sections.p: Each cell contains two copies of autosomal genes (one from each parent) and one or two sex‑chromosome copies. Mutations can be loss‑of‑function or gain‑of‑function, affecting protein activity.
b: Dominant mutations act even when a normal allele is present.
Recessive mutations need both alleles altered to manifest.
X‑linked genes escape inactivation in females, causing variable expression.

sections.p: Pathogenic variants disrupt normal protein function, leading to disease phenotypes that follow the inheritance rule of the mutated gene.
b: Huntington disease – autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion.
Cystic fibrosis – autosomal recessive CFTR loss‑of‑function.
Hemophilia A – X‑linked recessive factor VIII deficiency.
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy – mitochondrial DNA mutation.

sections.p: Understanding inheritance guides risk assessment, genetic testing, and family counseling, especially in low‑resource settings where targeted testing may be limited.
b: Take a three‑generation pedigree to spot dominant vs recessive patterns.
Identify carriers in consanguineous families to prevent recessive disease.
Consider mitochondrial disease when only maternal relatives are affected.

t.b: What pattern of transmission is present? Helps classify the disorder and estimate recurrence risk.
Does the patient carry the pathogenic variant? Positive result confirms diagnosis; negative may need broader panel.
Is a mtDNA mutation present? Positive supports mitochondrial disease; if unavailable, rely on clinical criteria and maternal history.

sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, key examples, and counseling points.
b: Dominant: vertical transmission, 50% risk to offspring.
Recessive: siblings affected, 25% risk to each child of carrier couple.
X‑linked recessive: males affected, carrier females 50% risk of sons being affected.

faq.q: How can I differentiate autosomal dominant from autosomal recessive on a pedigree?
faq.a: Dominant shows affected individuals in each generation; recessive often has unaffected parents with affected siblings.

faq.q: Why do mitochondrial diseases affect only children of affected mothers?
faq.a: Mitochondria are inherited solely from the oocyte; paternal mitochondria are discarded after fertilization.

faq.q: Can a carrier of an autosomal recessive disease ever show symptoms?
faq.a: Rarely, if the mutation has a mild dominant effect or if there is a second hit (e.g., environmental stress).

exam: Describe the inheritance pattern and give one example of an autosomal dominant and an autosomal recessive disorder.
Interpret a three‑generation pedigree showing vertical transmission and state the recurrence risk for offspring.
Explain why mitochondrial inheritance results in maternal transmission only.
